But as family structures evolve, another question is increasingly finding its way to the courts: who gets the pet? items.title: When criticism of a dead journalist turns into abuse, where is the line?
items.summary: Death is meant to be an exit, a full stop to the world’s qualms with a person. But on the internet, everything is up for scrutiny, whether or not the person can defend themselves anymore. After the untimely demise of noted Malayala Manorama journalist Jijo John Puthezhathu on September 9 in Kochi, the state has been witnessing an ethical paradox unfold– can the dead be mourned and still be condemned? In Jijo’s case, though, what is happening is more than condemnation. An onslaught of cruel cyber abuse targeting him and the integrity of his journalistic work has triggered police action at the request of his grieving family. The police have reportedly traced over 3000 abusive social media posts targeting him and humiliating his family on his behalf. The primary reason for the cyber lynching is that several people had quarrels with Jijo’s reporting, which is accused of being biased against the Left in Kerala. Some also allege his investigations for Malayalam Manorama to be targeted attacks on CPI(M)-leaning individuals and institutions, without enough evidence.
